title: Back a tow cart into its bay by the drawbar
instruction: First take the chock away from behind the cart's wheel, then back the cart rear-first into the green bay using only the orange drawbar handle, chock a wheel on its open side, and move both hands away. Don't jackknife or tip the cart, skid its wheels, or touch its body while it moves.
context: Warehouse and workshop staff back tow carts and tugger trailers into bays by the drawbar. Pushing a hinged, fixed-axle load in reverse is unstable: any error turns the cart further away, so a person has to steer it against the error, unlike pulling it or pushing a free cart. The demo plays a path computed in advance rather than correcting by eye.
setup: A workshop aisle on the table. A tow cart: a folded aluminium tray deck 13 x 9 cm, 3 to 4.5 cm above the table, carrying a blue plastic tote 11 x 8 cm with its top 7.5 cm up, 0.48 kg in all; two rubber wheels 4 cm across on a fixed axle, 16 cm apart; a nylon skid ball 2 cm across under the nose, 10 cm ahead of the axle. A drawbar hinged at a steel nose 12 cm ahead of the axle: an aluminium rod 1.2 cm square with an orange plastic handle 3 x 3 cm, 4 to 7.5 cm above the table, centred 10 cm from the hinge. The bar swings either way to a stop at 75 degrees, and up 20 degrees from level, where it rests when let go. The axle's middle stands at (22, 3) cm with the cart's nose and handle toward -y, between two grey painted lines 2 x 11 cm at x = 9.5 and 34.5 cm, running from y = -6 to 5 cm. A yellow aluminium chock, 190 g, a 4 cm square block 3 cm tall under a 2.5 cm square post with its top 7 cm up, stands at (14, 7.2) cm, 2 mm behind the wheel nearer the robot. The green bay faces it across the aisle: a green steel back stop 25 x 1 x 1.5 cm with its near face at y = 33.5 cm, centred at x = 34 cm, and green painted lines 2 x 11 cm at x = 21.5 and 46.5 cm, from y = 22.5 to 33.5 cm. Positions are from the arm bases' midpoint in x and the table's centre line in y, with +y toward the left arm. The screenshot shows the start.
scoring: Read at the end of the run. The cart's point is the middle of its axle on the table. A hand is a gripper's fingertip midpoint, and a part counts as let go only with both hands 6 cm or more from its box. 0 for good if: the bar reaches 70 degrees from the cart's axis (a jackknife); the cart tilts 6 degrees or its point rises 1.2 cm; its wheels skid sideways along the axle more than 3 cm in total, counting steps over 0.2 mm; the cart's nose turns 75 degrees or more from -y, which enforces rear-first travel, since a forward roll then always goes away from the bay; the cart shifts 5 mm or turns 3 degrees in total, added up over the trial, while a hand is within 6 cm of any part of it other than the handle (body, nose, axle, wheels or rod, each in its own frame; a hand counts as on the handle within 1.5 cm of its box); the cart shifts 2 cm or turns 8 degrees in total while a hand is on the chock (within 1.5 cm of its box) with the chock on the table within 6.5 cm of a wheel's centre, which up to that is chocking, not a hand on the cart; the cart moves 1.5 cm before the chock has been lifted 1 cm or moved so its centre is 8 cm from both wheels' centres; or the cart or chock leaves the table. Otherwise 0 until the cart's point has reached y = 9 cm, 6 cm toward the bay; 0.2 from there; 0.4 at y = 17 cm or more; 0.7 parked and let go: its point within 2.5 cm of (34, 31) cm in x and 3 cm in y, nose within 10 degrees of -y, both hands 6 cm from the handle and from every other part of the cart, unless on the chock; 0.9 also chocked and let go: the chock upright within 8 degrees and on the table, its centre 3.6 to 5.5 cm from a wheel's centre along the cart toward the hitch, within 2 cm of that wheel's line, judged in the cart's own frame. Either wheel will do. 1.0 with both also at rest (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s) and both hands clear of the cart and chock for the last 1 s.
reset_notes: Put the cart back at its start with the bar straight, and the chock behind the wheel. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: A rigid-body simulation. The wheels are free axle joints with ball-shaped colliders and real side grip, not a written constraint: measured yaw stayed within about 3 degrees of a bicycle model over the run, with no skid. The skid has near-zero friction and the joints a little drag. Real tyres, floor and bearings would differ, and the table stands in for a shop floor at scale. A grip is friction on a square handle; the bar is rigid.
